rule: A ✓ means a published, machine-checked proof shows that all the code computing the operation, as that library runs it on that host, gives the specified result for every input: the cipher and its mode, the hash over every block with its padding, the whole scalar multiplication or exponentiation, and the glue around them, such as clamping, byte conversion, and point encoding. Parsing DER key and signature containers, randomness, and the message hash a signature takes are left out. Proofs of memory safety alone, or of only some of the code, earn no ✓.

hosts.name: fedora
hosts.note: The maintainer's Fedora workstation and the report's only AVX-512 host, so the one whose table times rind's AVX-512 AES-GCM, IFMA RSA, and 8-way ML-KEM sampler against every library. Zen 5 keeps its clock with 512-bit vectors, so this host cannot show what they cost on the Intel cores that slow down.

hosts.name: kixtop
hosts.note: The maintainer's MacBook Air, in daily use. Its cores have DIT, and every rind row holds `rind::cpu::Dit::hold()` across calls, as MoQ does, so the rustls rows run rustls' own code with DIT on too. On every logical CPU, rind-rustls's handshakes gain less than aws-lc-rs's from the 6 efficiency cores: more of their time is multiplication-heavy assembly, which those cores run at 34-45% of a performance core's speed. The Air has no fan, so its performance cores slow within a minute there, giving those cores a larger share.
hosts.scaling: rind-rustls on all 10 logical CPUs runs full handshakes at 5.1 times and resumed handshakes at 4.8 times its one-thread rate.

hosts.name: ovh-iad
hosts.note: OVH VPS in Virginia, 4 shared vCPUs: other tenants add noise that a dedicated host's times lack.
hosts.scaling: rind-rustls on all 4 logical CPUs runs full handshakes at 3.5 times and resumed handshakes at 3.4 times its one-thread rate.

quest.title: Poly1305 runs a vectorized SSE2 path on x86_64 CPUs without SSE4.1

gaps.reason: Fixed, pending the weekly bench: the portable backend now bitslices eight blocks into SSE2 words on x86 and x86_64, as this row's aws-lc does ([steelhead99x/rind#352](https://github.com/steelhead99x/rind/pull/352)). On a shared 2-core x86_64 VM, AES-128 and AES-256 GCM, CTR, and CBC decryption at 1200 B and 16 KB took 0.67 to 1.05× aws-lc's time, from 1.20 to 1.88× before, and the four-block path's 88 instructions per CTR byte fell to 44. Remove this entry once a weekly run shows the row within 10%.

quest.title: The portable backend's SHA-1 is as fast as aws-lc's integer code

gaps.reason: Unwrapping a 16-byte AES-128 key takes 39 ns more than aws-lc-rs's 323 ns on the EPYC 7763 runner of [run 44941104585](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/actions/runs/44941104585), 1.12× its time, as it took 1.11 to 1.20× on the EPYC runners of the run before; the Xeon 6975P native tier unwraps it in 0.95× aws-lc-rs's time, wrapping, every longer key, and the other tiers are within 10%, and aarch64 unwraps in 0.68×. Key wrap is rare and runs once per stored key, so the fixed cost stays without a quest; the next refresh rechecks it.

Decided in [kixel-ai/rind#812](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/812): on x86_64 without AVX-512, ML-KEM-768 key generation stays on rind's arithmetic though pyca/verified-garbage's is faster, since a key pair decapsulates on the arithmetic that generated it and VG's decapsulation was 1.17 to 1.25× slower there when it decided, and decapsulation is the hot path. `desktop`'s Arrow Lake narrows that: VG generated keys in 4.83 µs against rind's 6.51 and decapsulated in 4.74 against 4.51 (1.05×). aarch64 holds for the same reason: on `kixtop`'s Apple M4 VG generated keys in 5.22 µs against rind's 6.36 but decapsulated in 4.79 against 4.21 (1.14×), and `ovh-iad` and `ovh-sea` decapsulated at 1.16 and 1.21× rind's time.

quest.title: AES-GCM on Intel without AVX-512 runs verified-garbage's code for long messages where it is faster

gaps.reason: Noise: 1.11× pyca/verified-garbage's time on `fedora` (160 against 145 ns) in its first run on two reserved cores, with the other 28 of 32 CPUs busy, but 1.06× in a recheck of the same commit (153 ns) and 1.03× in its quiet run of 2026-11-24, and rind runs the same code at every size, where 1350 B and 16 KB stayed within 10%.

1.13× graviola's time on `fedora` (5.06 against 4.44 µs) in its first run on two reserved cores, and 1.13× in a recheck, against 1.03× in its quiet run of 2026-11-24 (4.24 against 4.12). rind runs pyca/verified-garbage's AVX-512 decapsulation here, whose own row took 4.71 µs (1.07× rind's glue, against 1.01× then), and no change to that path's code landed between the runs. Every library slowed with the other 28 of 32 CPUs busy, graviola's AVX2 code least (8%, against VG's 13% and rind's 19%), so the host's shared power budget is the likely cause; the next refresh rechecks it, and a second run at this margin gets a quest.

1.11× pyca/verified-garbage's time on `ovh-iad` (66.2 against 59.5 µs), and 1.08× in its other quiet run of the same commit, 1.17× on `desktop` (19.7 against 16.9 µs; aws-lc-rs 46.7) on two reserved cores, as in its quiet run before, and 1.08× on `nixos` (29.7 against 27.4 µs; 1.11× and 1.08× in its last two quiet runs), while `ovh-sea` measured 1.06× and `fedora` 1.09× (19.1 against 17.4 µs). rind already runs VG's `d·G` for each signature's `k·G` ([#847](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/847)), so the difference is in rind's other steps, among them its hedged nonce: fresh randomness for each signature, as aws-lc-rs draws, where VG derives its nonce deterministically by RFC 6979. That behavior is deliberate, so it stays; the next refresh rechecks the margin.

Noise: other tenants share `ovh-iad`'s VPS, whose load the report cannot see. rind took 539 ns against pyca/verified-garbage's 482 (1.12×), where its previous refresh measured 498 against the same 482 (1.03×) on the same SHA-3 code, and `ovh-sea` measured 1.03× (472 against 457), with SHA3-512 at 64 B 1.05× on both. The next refresh rechecks it.

quest.title: ChaCha20-Poly1305 on Intel without AVX-512 runs verified-garbage's code where it is faster

gaps.reason: Deliberate: pyca/verified-garbage runs the SHA512 instructions on `desktop`'s Arrow Lake, taking 0.24 to 0.66 of rind's time, and rind does not, since Intel's data-independent-timing list omits `VSHA512RNDS2`, `VSHA512MSG1`, and `VSHA512MSG2` (PLATFORMS.md). rind's AVX2 routine still beats every other library there, at 0.87 to 0.99 of the next fastest's time.

Deliberate: these rows time rind without a `rind::cpu::Dit::hold()` guard, so it sets DIT around each call, which took 33 to 43 ns a call on `kixtop`'s Apple M4 (52.3 against 9.33 ns to seal 32 B with AES-128-GCM while holding it, 187 against 154 with ChaCha20-Poly1305). The other libraries leave DIT off, so their times buy no data-independent timing. A caller making many short calls holds the guard, as MoQ does, and rind's own rows show that cost gone.

Not yet re-measured: the weekly data predates verification adding first and checking for equal points only at a zero z ([kixel-ai/rind#1074](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/1074)), after which this row took 1.075× aws-lc-rs's time on the tier's Xeon 6975P-C, against 1.15× before; a Core Ultra 7 270K with ADX denied measured 1.12× before and after. What remains is setup for a key used once, the inversion and batch conversion that make P to 15P affine, which aws-lc-rs skips. Keeping them Jacobian, or building only P to 7P, measured no faster on x86_64, so the setup stays.

[kixel-ai/rind#1035](https://github.com/kixel-ai/rind/pull/1035) copies the key in constant-size moves, which removed a store-forwarding stall that AES-192 alone paid, 10 ns of its 112; the next refresh rechecks it.
